item.title: Apprenticeship in Switzerland: contracts, salary and maturity
item.description: Internship contracts, remuneration, compulsory contributions and professional maturity: an apprenticeship guide in the Swiss training system.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Apprenticeship lasts 3-4 years and combines practical work and school education - AVS/AI contributions: 5.3% for the apprentice (10.6% for employer) - Minimum holidays: 4 weeks (5 under 20 years old) - Federal contract: the same rights in every Swiss canton
## Key facts - **What**: Dual education system that alternates practical work and vocational school - Where: All Swiss cantons, including Basel-Landschaft - Who: Young people from 15 years old and up - Duration: 3-4 years depending on the professional field - Mandatory contributions: AVS/AI 5.3% (employee), 10.6% (employer) - Maximum hours: 45 hours/week (industry, offices, sales) or 50 in other sectors
Apprenticeship is the heart of the Swiss vocational education system. It represents a path combining education and work: the student spends approximately 3-4 days a week in the company and one-two days in vocational school. In the canton of Basel-Landschaft, as in other cantons, the system follows uniform federal rules that define rights, duties and protections for anyone undertaking this path.
The apprenticeship contract is the fundamental document. Regulated by federal law, it must contain the company's data, the apprentice's details, the professional sector, the start date, the total duration, the weekly hours and the remuneration. Once signed by the company and apprentice (with parents or whoever exercises parental authority, if a minor), the contract acquires legal validity.
Working hours must not exceed 45 hours per week in industry, offices and sales, or 50 hours in other sectors. The apprentice is entitled to a minimum of 4 weeks of annual holidays — 5 weeks if under 20. These protections are guaranteed by federal law and apply uniformly in all cantons.
### How the remuneration system works
The apprentice's remuneration is established in the apprenticeship contract. There is no federal minimum wage, although many cantons have defined regional ones and several sectors have collective agreements. During the salary, the apprentice automatically pays 5.3% of AVS/AI contributions (the employer adds 10.6% to their account). Additionally, 1.1% up to the annual limit goes to unemployment insurance (UIC/UCA).
Accident insurance (LAINF/LAI) ranges between 0.7% and 1.5% depending on the sector of activity and is covered by the employer. The LPP pension system (second pillar) usually does not apply to apprentices, as the remuneration is often below the coordination threshold. With the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) online it is possible to estimate net and charges on a hypothetical remuneration. ### Rights and protections during training
The traineeship contract must be filed with the competent cantonal office — in the canton of Basel-Country with the Vocational Training Office. The apprentice always receives a signed copy of the contract. If during the probationary period (usually 1-3 months) incompatibilities arise between the young person and the employer, the contract may be terminated with 1 week's notice by both parties.
After the probationary period, cancellation times are tightened: 1 month in the first year of apprenticeship, 2 months from the second to the ninth year, 3 months from the tenth year onwards. These times are established by federal law and apply in each canton.
Social contributions represent an important voice for those who hire an apprentice. On the one hand, the young person sees 5.3% of AVS/AI and 1.1% of AD/AC deducted from his net; on the other, the employer pays 10.6% of AVS/AI, 1.1% of AD/AC and the cost of LAINF/LAA accident insurance (0.7%-1.5% depending on the sector). All these payments are mandatory by federal law and identical in each canton.
### Health insurance and taxes
Health insurance (LAMal/KVG) is mandatory for anyone residing in Switzerland. The apprentice must stipulate it within 3 months of the start of the training. Premiums are determined by canton and tariff region; the canton Basel-Country has its own tariffs. Adult deductibles range from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500 depending on plan
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Professional Maturity: Additional Qualification
Professional maturity is an additional qualification that apprentices can obtain in parallel with their apprenticeship or immediately after its conclusion. It consists of theoretical lessons in general subjects — languages, mathematics, history, economics, sciences — along with the practical training in the company. At the end of the apprenticeship, the young person obtains both the certificate of competence (AFC, federal apprenticeship diploma) and, if they have attended the mandatory courses, the professional maturity certificate.
Professional maturity is recognized at the federal level and is a privileged gateway to access professional university schools (SUP). Many cantons, including Basel-Landschaft, offer maturity courses at ordinary professional schools. The cost is usually free or minimal for the apprentice; the school is financed by the canton itself. Completing professional maturity simultaneously with the apprenticeship requires organization, but allows for further qualification without extending the overall training time.
### How to Find and Start an Apprenticeship
Searching for an apprenticeship position takes place mainly through national and regional job advertisement portals, the local employment office, direct contacts with companies in the field of interest, and school orientation fairs. Once a potential employer is found, the negotiation of the apprenticeship contract proceeds.
Before signing, it is essential to verify that the document contains: the name and address of the company, the name and date of birth of the apprentice, the professional branch, start date, total duration in years, declared weekly hours, monthly or annual remuneration and payment methods. The cantonal professional education office of Basel-Landschaft can provide advice on contractual standards and minimum rights.
### Next Steps
To navigate the world of apprenticeships and estimate your net salary after contributions and taxes, use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator). To search for apprenticeship offers in the canton of Basel-Landschaft, access specialized [job board](nav:jobs) portals, which allow you to filter by region, sector, and type of training. If you have questions about contracts, rights, hours, or contributions during the apprenticeship, the cantonal professional education office remains the main reference.

item.title: Family allowances Canton Basel Countryside: amounts and demand
item.description: How to request them, monthly amounts per child, conditions and compensation fund: practical guide to family allowances in the Canton of Basel-Country.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell

## Key facts
- **What**: Family and training allowances in the canton of Basel-Country - Where: Canton Basel Countryside (cantonal clearing house) - Who: Parents residing and employees in the canton - When: Application to be submitted to the competent office (deadlines check locally) - Type: Federal benefit administered at cantonal level
Family allowances in the canton of Basel-Country are part of the Swiss federal family support system. These are periodic benefits intended for parents for each fiscally dependent child. The entitlement to family allowances and the related monthly amounts vary depending on the canton of residence and the economic situation of the family. In the canton of Basel-Country, as in the other Swiss cantons, there is a territorially competent clearing house in charge of handling claims and payments.
### Who is entitled to family allowances
In Switzerland, entitlement to family allowances is granted to parents and other entitled persons in accordance with federal rules coordinated with cantonal legislation. In the canton of Basel-Country, ### Application Procedure and Deadlines
To claim family allowances in the canton of Basel-Country, you must contact the territorially competent compensation fund. The procedure can be carried out online (if available), or by means of a paper form to be filed with the local office of the clearing house or with the municipal administration of residence.
The application must include identity documents, children's birth certificates, school or training certificates (for training allowances), and documentation of the family's financial situation, if requested. It is advisable to acquire the exact list of documents at the competent office, as requests may vary depending on the type of benefit and family situation.
### Monthly amounts per child
The amounts of family allowances in the canton of Basel-Country are fixed by cantonal law. In the federal system, each canton independently defines the monthly amounts for each dependent child. These amounts may vary depending on the birth order of the child (first child, second child, third child and subsequent) and may be differentiated by standard family allowances and training allowances.
The amounts specific to the Canton of Basel-Country (for example: CHF XXX for the first child, CHF XXX for the second, etc.) must be verified at the cantonal clearing house or at the site

Step 2: Obtain the Application Form Download the application form from the compensation fund's website or the cantonal administration's website, or pick it up from the physical office. The form is usually available in PDF or hard copy format.
**Step 3: Complete the Application** Fill in the form with personal data, children's information (name, date of birth, AVS insurance number, if applicable), economic and employment situation. Attach the requested documents (birth certificates, school certificates, training certificates, income documentation).
Step 4: Submit the Application Send the completed application electronically (if the compensation fund offers online services), by regular mail, or deliver it in person to the compensation fund's office or the competent municipal office.
Step 5: Follow Up on the Application The compensation fund will communicate the outcome of the request by letter. The first payment usually occurs within 30-60 days of the application's acceptance, based on the fund's internal procedures.
### Additional Information and Contacts To know the exact amounts of family allowances and training allowances in the Canton of Basel-Country, any supplements, deadlines, and payment methods, please contact directly: - The competent compensation fund for your municipality of residence - The cantonal administration office responsible for family benefits - Your municipality of residence, which can provide guidance on cantonal services

The Federal Road Traffic Act requires foreign residents to convert their licence into a Swiss licence within specified time limits. In the Canton of Basel-City, this procedure is managed by the Traffic Office (Amt für Verkehr), which supervises the theoretical and practical examinations necessary for homologation.

The test covers specific topics such as precedence, safety distances, behaviour in adverse weather conditions, load rules, speed limitations, and use of on-board technology.
The practical exam is a road test with an official observer assessing your driving skills in real-world settings. They check coordination, compliance with rules, perception of danger, and behavior in traffic. Both exams must be passed to obtain a Swiss licence.

item.title: DEFR: new forms for transfers to Iran
item.description: On 19 August, the Federal Department of Economic Affairs adapted the declaration forms. From 26 August, only updated models will be mandatory.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - DEFR adapted the forms on 19 August 2026 - From 26 August only new models will be accepted - Relates to transfers of assets according to art. 21 of the Iran order
## Key facts - **What**: Modification of declaration and authorization forms for transfers of assets - When: Adaptation 19 August 2026; mandatory application from 26 August 2026 - Where: Bern, Federal Department of Economics - Who: DEFR (Federal Department of Economics, Training and Research) - Reference: Art. 21 order measures against the Islamic Republic of Iran
On 19 August 2026, the Federal Department of Economic Affairs, Training and Research (DEFR) made a major change to the administrative forms for transfers of assets. The decision concerns in particular the declaration and authorisation forms governed by Article 21 of the Ordinance instituting measures against the Islamic Republic of Iran.
### The date of mandatory application As of August 26, 2026, only the appropriate forms according to the modified version will be accepted. This means that anyone who has to transfer capital to Iran, as of that date, must use the new forms. The time window between the announcement (August 19) and the entry into force (August 26) allows a seven-day transition for administrative managers, Swiss banks and citizens ### Who is affected by the change This administrative change concerns anyone who needs to transfer funds to the Islamic Republic of Iran in accordance with Swiss federal rules. These are not only companies that trade with the country, but also individual Swiss citizens who maintain financial relations abroad or who must transfer capital to family members or beneficiaries in Iran. Non-profit organizations and entities with offices in Switzerland also fall within the scope of the law.
### Impact on banking procedures Swiss banks authorized to make international transfers will have to update their processing systems to verify that customers only fill out and submit forms in the version of August 19, 2026. Credit institutions will have the task of checking the compliance of the documentation and rejecting any requests based on obsolete forms. This could result in slower processing times during the first transition period.
### Prevent administrative errors The nature of the change makes it essential to acquire the correct forms promptly. Those who delay the retrieval of updated documentation risk finding themselves in the situation of not being able to make transfers in the period immediately following 26 August, if they are still using the previous forms. Organizations that handle transfers
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Step-by-Step Practical Procedure To comply with the new regulations before the August 26 deadline, it is advisable to follow these steps. First, access the official DEFR website and download the forms in the modified version of August 19, 2026. Do not delay this operation beyond August 25. Second, if you operate through a Swiss bank, contact the customer service or compliance office to verify that the institution has already integrated the new modules into its processing systems. Third, review the technical compilation specifications provided by the DEFR together with the updated forms, as there may be variations in the required fields compared to the previous version.
### Pre-Application Checklist Before August 26, 2026, make sure you have completed the following requirements: have you downloaded the updated forms from the DEFR portal? Have you verified which is the correct version? Have you contacted your bank to confirm that it accepts the new modules? Have you fully completed the required documentation? Have you prepared backup copies for your records and for the bank? Have you informed your beneficiaries in Iran, if necessary, about any possible procedural delays? Have you checked for any changes in processing times during the transition phase?
### Next Actions Do not delay the completion of the new forms beyond August 25, 2026. Federal administrations and banks will apply the new procedure strictly from the date of entry into force. If you need assistance in managing the tax treatment of international transfers, [consult our salary and tax calculator](nav:calculator) to verify your tax burden in Switzerland. For further information on your rights and duties in completing federal administrative documentation, contact the DEFR directly or your banking institution.

item.title: Labour market Basel City: wages, sectors and contracts
item.description: Guide to wage levels by education level, hiring sectors, collective agreements and labour market mechanisms in the Canton of Basel-City.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Salaries in the Canton of Basel-City vary significantly depending on the sector and the level of vocational training - Switzerland has no federal minimum wage; wage protections are based on cantonal and sectoral collective agreements - The Swiss labour market requires mandatory affiliation to AVS/AI, LPP and LAMal for residents and employees
## Key facts - **System**: The Swiss labour market operates on three pillars (federal, cantonal, municipal) - Wage protection: No federal minimum wage; protection through cantonal/sectoral collective agreements (CCL) - Contributions: Employees pay AVS/AI 5.3%, AD/AC 1.1%, LAINF 0.7–1.5% according to sector - Hourly flexibility: Max 45 hours/week (industry, offices, sales) or 50 in other sectors - Minimum holidays: At least 4 weeks per year (5 under 20); cancellation deadlines: 1/2/3 months
The labour market in the Canton of Basel-City reflects the general structure of the Swiss system, where wages and conditions of employment are not regulated by a single federal law, but by a complex of collective agreements at sectoral and cantonal level. Unlike other European countries, Switzerland does not have a minimum wage set by federal law. This means that wage protection depends entirely on negotiated agreements between employers and trade unions.
### Wage structure and training levels
In the Canton of Basel-City, as throughout the ### How wage contributions work in Switzerland
For those working in the Canton of Basel-City, the gross salary indicated in a contract is subject to compulsory reductions due to social contributions. These are not taxes in the traditional sense, but funding for social protection systems run by federal agencies.
The ** AVS/AI system ** (Old Age and Survivors Insurance/Disability Insurance) is the first pillar of Swiss social security. Employees and employers each pay 5.3% of gross salary to these schemes. Unemployment insurance (AD) and occupational accident insurance (AC) add an additional 1.1% up to an annual cap. Non-occupational accident insurance (LAINF) varies from 0.7 to 1.5% depending on the sector of activity.
The second pillar, occupational pension (LPP — Law on occupational pension for old age, survivors and disability), is mandatory for those who earn above a minimum coordination threshold. LPP contributions start at 7% of the coordinated salary (for workers aged 25–34) and increase significantly with age: 10% for those aged 35–44, 15% for those aged 45–54, and 18% for those aged 55 up to the reference retirement age. These contributions are generally divided between employee and employer, although the exact distribution depends on the internal regulations of the fund of
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### What to do concretely: step-by-step for job seekers in the Basel City Canton Step 1: Verify your qualification and applicable collective contract Before negotiating a job offer, identify the collective contract (CCL) applicable to the sector and position of interest. If the employer claims to operate under a specific CCL (e.g., the Basel City chemical-pharmaceutical CCL), ensure the proposed salary respects the minimum wages and benefits outlined in the contract. Many employers provide this document upon explicit request. If they don’t indicate a CCL, it doesn’t mean one doesn’t exist: verify with the trade association or local unions. Step 2: Calculate net salary from gross Upon receiving a job offer with a monthly gross salary, deduct mandatory social contributions (AVS/AI, AD/AC, LAINF) to estimate the net. Then, approximate the federal, cantonal, and communal direct taxes: Basel City has its own tax rates, differing from other cantons. Use an [online salary calculator](nav:calculator) for a realistic net estimate, noting the result is indicative and depends on personal deductions (rent, health insurance, LPP contributions). Step 3: Understand LPP (Pension Plan) Benefits Request a copy of the company’s LPP regulations from the employer and verify the employee’s vs. employer’s contribution percentage. The federal rule (7–18% of coordinated salary) is a legal minimum; many qualified companies in Basel City offer better conditions. Clarify the “coordination deduction” amount (minimum salary threshold included in LPP calculations), which the employer must communicate transparently. Step 4: Subscribe to LAMal within legal deadlines If not already insured, purchase health insurance within 3 months of starting employment in Basel City. Choose a deductible suitable for your risk profile. Check if Basel City offers subsidies to reduce premiums based on the previous year’s declared income. This is a right, not a favor: formally request it from cantonal authorities if your income is low. **Step 5: Register with AVS** The employer typically registers the employee with the local Old Age and Survivors’ Insurance (AVS) Office. However, it’s advisable to verify within the first weeks that the AVS number has been assigned and contributions have started. This prevents gaps in your contribution record that could reduce your future pension. Step 6: Understand notice and termination rights Before accepting a contract, carefully read the notice terms. While federal law provides for 1/2/3 months’ notice based on seniority, individual contracts might include longer or shorter terms (usually longer). If terminated during the first month of probation, it’s generally possible to interrupt with short notice: check the contract. Always document final employment term agreements in writing. ### Useful Resources and Links To delve deeper into the Swiss salary and pension system applicable to Basel City, use this site’s [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to estimate your net and understand the weight of contributions. Basel City also publishes main collective contracts online and references to local public administrations handling taxation and subsidies. In Summary: Basel City’s job market operates under Swiss federal rules for salary protection, pension, and taxation, with sectors like chemical-pharmaceutical and finance traditionally offering higher compensation. The key to negotiating knowingly is understanding the applicable collective contract, calculating the true net salary, and timely registration in mandatory pension systems. Doing so from the first day of employment avoids surprises and ensures legal protection.

item.description: System of contributions, hours and workers' rights in the canton of Basel-City: federal rules, compulsory social security and cantonal rules for those working in Switzerland.

## In a nutshell - **No federal minimum wage ** in Switzerland or Basel City - AVS/AI contributions: 5.3% on employee salary, 10.6% total with employer - Maximum hours: 45 hours/week (industry, offices), 50 hours in other sectors - Minimum holidays: 4 weeks a year, 5 for children under 20
## Key facts - What: Social security structure and workers' rights in Switzerland - Where: Canton Basel-City (CH) - Who: All employees and employers - AVS/AI/IPG contributions: 5.3% employee (total 10.6% with employer) - LPP contributions: 7% (25–34 years), 10% (35–44), 15% (45–54), 18% (55+ reference age) - Hours: 45–50 hours/week according to sector
The labour market in the canton of Basel-City is governed by an overlap of federal rules and cantonal provisions that directly affect wages, social contributions and conditions of employment. Unlike neighbouring countries, Switzerland does not set a minimum wage at the federal level. Nor does the canton of Basel-City impose a uniform legal minimum wage: salaries are formed through individual contracts and, where provided, collective labour agreements (CCAs) in the various sectors.
However, the structure of compulsory contributions is standardised at national level. Each employee pays 5.3% of the gross salary in AVS/AI/IPG contributions (old age and disability insurance, loss of earnings allowance). The employer pays an amount ## How wages are structured in Switzerland
In Basel City, as in the rest of Switzerland, there is no legal minimum wage obligation at the cantonal level. This means that the salary is negotiated directly between employer and worker, or is regulated by a collective agreement if the sector so provides. Some Swiss sectors (construction, catering, healthcare, construction) have CCAs that set minimum wages. Basel-City, being an industrial and commercial canton, has strong CCA presences in the manufacturing and service sectors.
The cost of work for the employer is lower than the gross salary of the employee: he must add the AVS/AI contributions (10.6%), the accident insurance premiums (0.7%–1.5% depending on the sector), and the LPP contribution (minimum 50% of the rate prescribed by the fund). These fixed costs directly affect the total salary that the company must allocate for each position.
On the worker side, annual gross salary is reduced by AVS/AI personal contributions (5.3%) and by LPP contributions (7%–18% depending on age). Federal and cantonal taxes are deducted from these. Basel-City has its own cantonal tax rate: the system is progressive, and the amount depends on salary, marital status and number of children. It is not uncommon for a worker in Basel City to have his annual gross reduced by about 25%–35% due to taxes and mandatory contributions.

item.title: Wages and work in Switzerland: training levels
item.description: How Swiss wages work by level of training, compulsory social contributions, collective agreements and cantonal minimum wage.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - AVS/AI/IPG contributions amount to 5.3% for the employee (10.6% with the employer) - The maximum hours are 45 hours per week in industry, offices and sales; 50 in other sectors - The LPP provides for pension contributions from 7% to 18% of the coordinated salary according to age - Some cantons have their own minimum wage; Switzerland has no federal minimum
## Key facts - **What**: Compulsory wage structure and social security contributions in Switzerland - Who: Employees, employers, Federal Office of Social Security (UFAS/BSV) - Where: Entire Swiss territory (national + cantonal regulations) - When: Continuous application; amounts indexed annually - AVS contribution: 5.3% employee + 5.3% employer (total 10.6%) - LPP age 25-34: Minimum 7% of the coordinated salary
The Swiss labour market is based on a wage structure that is strictly regulated at federal and cantonal level. Those who work in Switzerland automatically pay mandatory contributions for old-age and survivors' insurance (AVS), disability insurance (AI) and unemployment insurance (IPG). These three contributions amount to 5.3% of the gross salary for the employee, while the employer pays an identical share, for a total of 10.6%.
To these are added contributions for family allowances (variable amount according to the canton), accident insurance (LAINF/LAA, between 0.7% and 1.5% according to the sector of ## Training, qualifications and salary levels
In Switzerland, the link between level of education and salary level is direct. Those who have an apprenticeship certification (initial vocational training, AFC) have access to different salary levels than those who have completed high school, and still different from those who have graduated from a university or polytechnic school. However, the SOURCE CONTENT does not specify precise minimum wage figures by degree of training, because the Swiss system does not have a single national minimum wage.
### Minimum Wage: Federal Absence and Cantonal Diversity
Unlike many European countries, Switzerland does not have a federal law setting a national minimum wage. This means that the minimum wage protection is managed by the individual cantons and, in some cases, by collective labour agreements (CCLs). Some cantons have introduced their own cantonal minimum wages; others rely entirely on collective agreements and the market. For those who work or are looking for a job in Switzerland, it is therefore essential to check the regulations of the canton of residence or employment.
Collective labour agreements play a central role in determining wages and conditions of employment. These agreements are negotiated between trade unions (on the one hand) and employers' associations (on the other) and set minimum wages, wage increases, working hours, public holidays and additional benefits for entire sectors
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## How to navigate the Swiss salary system: concrete actions
Anyone starting a job in Switzerland or already working and looking to negotiate a promotion needs to understand the practical workings of the salary package. A typical Swiss salary package shows:
1. **Gross salary**: the amount agreed upon in the employment contract 2. Deductions (AVS/AI/IPG 5.3%, LPP according to age and coordination, LAINF/LAA 0.7-1.5%, VAT if due, any salary tax) 3. Net salary: what remains after all deductions
To verify the accuracy of your salary package, it's a good idea to consult the applicable rates in your canton and industry. The SECO (State Secretariat for Economic Affairs) and the cantonal offices of social security provide free online calculators.
### Step 1: Check the cantonal minimum salary
Before negotiating or accepting a job offer, check the cantonal administration website to see if there is a minimum salary in your canton. If not, consult the applicable collective labor agreement (available on union or employer association websites).
### Step 2: Calculate the coordinated salary for LPP
The coordinated salary is not the gross salary, but a technical concept: gross salary minus a fixed deduction (the amount of which is adjusted annually). From this coordinated salary, the pension contributions are deducted according to your age group. Use the pension funds' or your employer's online calculators to get precise estimates.
### Step 3: Collective labor agreements and salary protection
If your industry has a collective labor agreement, read it carefully to see what benefits are included, such as annual pay increases, performance bonuses, 13th month, sick leave benefits, and other non-visible benefits in the basic salary. Unions and employer associations provide free consultations on the correct application of collective labor agreements.
### Step 4: Plan the third pillar (third pillar 3a)
In addition to AVS/AHV (first pillar) and LPP/BVG (second pillar), Swiss workers can voluntarily contribute to a [third pillar 3a](nav:pillar3) for supplementary pension savings with tax benefits. The maximum amount that can be contributed is adjusted annually and is different for employees with or without LPP.
## Practical implications: what to check before signing
Before signing a contract, make sure you:
- Know your monthly or annual gross salary and check that it is equal to or higher than the cantonal minimum (if it exists) - Understand which pension fund manages LPP and what rate will be applied - Check if your contract is covered by a collective labor agreement - Check the estimated net salary using an online calculator - Inform yourself about the statutory notice period if you want to terminate the employment relationship in the future
The Swiss labor market protects employees through central and standardized federal regulations, as well as cantonal and union-level negotiations. Understanding these rules means protecting yourself and negotiating your contract consciously.

## In a nutshell - The compensation fund manages AVS contributions (5.3% employees, 10.6% total with employer) - Contribution gaps reduce future income by as much as 1-2% per missing year - Complementary services fill the gap between income and cantonal minimum wage

## First pillar and cantonal compensation fund
The cantonal compensation fund of the Canton of Basel-City is the entity responsible for the concrete management of the first pillar of social security, namely Old-Age and Survivors' Insurance (AVS). It is not a personal savings fund, but a solidarity contribution system: those who work pay AVS contributions (5.3% for employees, 10.6% total with the employer's contribution) that directly finance the pensions of current pensioners.
The fund collects these contributions through the salary and pays them to the Confederation, which then redistributes the funds to the cantonal funds on the basis of demographic needs and income demands. At the same time, the cantonal fund calculates and pays old-age, survivors' and ## Complementary services and minimum life expectancy in the canton
When the AVS annuity is not sufficient to cover the cost of living, supplementary benefits (PC) intervene. In the Canton of Basel-City, supplementary benefits are provided by the Department of Health and Social Affairs (DSS) in coordination with the cantonal compensation fund.
Supplementary benefits are not a charitable welfare measure, but a right enshrined in the Federal Act on Supplementary Benefits to AVH and AI (LPPC). Any resident who reaches retirement age and does not have sufficient income can make use of it.
### The concept of vital minimum
PCs calculate the difference between disposable income (AVS income + other income from work, rent or property, private pensions, AI annuities) and the ** living minimum ** recognized in the canton. The living minimum covers rent, food, energy, communications, local transport and essential needs.
In 2026, the reference federal minimum wage remains indexed annually according to the SVP (Business Statistics) wage index. Those living in the City of Basel and approaching retirement age must follow a precise procedure to ensure they do not lose money owed and obtain the optimal combination of AVS and PC. Here are the concrete steps.
### Step 1: Request an Individual Account (Versichertenkonto)
At least 4–6 months before the scheduled retirement date, contact the cantonal compensation fund of the City of Basel to request your individual account (Versichertenkonto / Dossier individuel). This document summarizes:
- All contributions paid since the first job to date - Any gaps and non-covered periods - The average income calculated according to the federal formula
The request is free and can be made online, by mail, or in person at the counter. The fund will send the account within 2–3 weeks.
### Step 2: Verify and Fill Gaps in Contributions
By examining the account, identify any gaps. If present and dating back to the last 5 years, it is possible to pay voluntary retroactive contributions. The fund provides an estimate of the amount due.
For periods of indemnified unemployment, the unemployment insurance (AD/AC) automatically covers contributions, so no manual intervention is required.
For other missing periods (periods abroad, non-indemnified illness), retroactive payment is optional but highly recommended: each year filled increases the future pension by approximately 2–2.5%.
### Step 3: Obtain the Pension Simulation
The cantonal compensation fund provides a written simulation of the estimated AVS pension based on current data. This document indicates:
- The gross monthly pension amount - Deductions (LAMal contributions, if applicable) - The effective net amount
The simulation is binding for the fund; it allows for planning the pension budget and evaluating whether it will be necessary to apply for PC.
### Step 4: Submit a Request for Supplementary Benefits (if necessary)
If the simulated pension does not reach the cantonal minimum, submit a request for PC by the month in which the retirement age is reached. The request must be filed with the PC office of the City of Basel (Department of Health and Social Affairs, DSS).
Required documentation:
- Lease agreement and payment receipts (last 3 months) - Income tax declaration (last 2 fiscal years) - Bank statement extracts (last 2 months) - Property certificate (if owner-occupied) - Active LAMal policy for each family member - Certificate of absence of significant assets (if required)
### Step 5: Follow the Liquidation
The cantonal compensation fund liquidates the AVS pension from the first day of the month following the retirement age (or the chosen date if it is postponed). The amount is paid monthly to a designated bank account.
The PC office communicates the decision on the request for supplementary benefits within 30–45 days. If approved, the PC is paid simultaneously with the AVS pension.
### Free Support and Counseling
The cantonal compensation fund of the City of Basel offers completely free counseling throughout all stages. It is possible to contact the office by phone, email, or in person. Many funds also provide digital counseling and downloadable information material online.
Alternative: the SVP (Voluntary Service for Pensioners) counters in many municipalities offer free voluntary assistance with filling out forms and preparing the application.
For those who want to deepen the pension calculation and understand the AVS/PC system better, it is possible to use the [federal AVS calculator](nav:pension) available on the UFAS/BSV website. For tax-related issues related to the pension, consult the cantonal tax administration of the City of Basel.

## Key facts

On August 19, 2026, the Federal Council communicated an update relevant to anyone conducting international economic operations. The SESAM database, the Swiss Federal Sanctions Management System, has been updated to reflect the changes made by the UN Sanctions Committee to the lists of individuals, businesses and organisations subject to restrictive measures. An event that might seem purely technical, but which has concrete implications for millions of transactions involving Switzerland.
This update is not an isolated event. It represents the application of a structural decision of the Federal Council dated 4 March 2016. On that date, the Swiss Executive approved an order establishing the automatic transposition of the lists of ### Who is subject to verification obligations
The network of Swiss subjects who have to check the SESAM database before making international transactions is much wider than you might imagine. It's not just about ** financial institutions ** and large multinationals. Anyone in Switzerland who transfers funds abroad, receives international payments, imports goods or participates in commercial transactions abroad enters a potential risk zone if they do not verify the counterparty in the SESAM list.
This includes [aziende piccole e medie](nav:companies), professionals (consultants, accountants, lawyers), traders, real estate entrepreneurs negotiating with foreign clients. Individuals who, for example, receive an international wire transfer or intend to invest funds abroad should also be aware that their contractor could appear on the list and make the transaction illegal.
Swiss banks and financial institutions, in particular, carry out systematic and automatic checks. Their systems are connected to SESAM and verify every transaction in real time. When the list is updated, such as August 19, 2026, these systems adjust immediately without manual intervention.
### Implications of Automatic Compliance
The immediate incorporation of UN sanctions into Swiss law has a fundamental practical consequence: there is no room for “I didn't know” or “I hadn't seen the update yet”. From the moment in which the

The SESAM database is publicly accessible on the Federal Administration website. Access is free and does not require registration; anyone can consult it from any internet-connected device.

### Monitoring and ongoing compliance
Compliance with UN sanctions is not a one-off burden, but a continuous one. item.title: Discriminatory announcement Zurich: what the LPar provides
item.description: A carpenter's shop in Zurich posted an ad with gender and age criteria. A lawyer explains what Swiss discrimination law provides for.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - A carpenter in the Canton of Zurich sought a secretary "preferably non-smoker, between 22 and 40 years old" - The announcement sparked an online debate: those who felt excluded protested - A labor law expert confirms that the ad is admissible under federal law
## Key facts - **What**: Job advertisement with criteria of gender, age and smoking habits - When: August 2026 - Where: Canton Zurich (Switzerland) - Who: Carpentry + Prof. Roger Rudolph (University of Zurich, labour law) - Applicable rule: Federal Law on Gender Equality (LPar) - Maximum allowance: Three monthly salary payments
### The case of Zurich carpentry
A carpenter's shop in the canton of Zurich has published a job advertisement for an administrative secretary who immediately ignited the online debate. The requirements were specific: "Preferably non-smoker, age about 22-40 years". In addition, due to the “already predominant male presence” in the team, a female person was desired.
The announcement drew criticism especially among those who felt excluded beforehand: men and smokers protested on social networks. Contacted by 20 Minuten, the carpenter chose not to make public statements. The question that many have asked themselves was immediate: to what extent is it legal to ask for such specific characteristics in a Swiss job advertisement?
### The assessment ### When discrimination is triggered in the hiring phase
According to Professor Rudolph, if a man applies despite the indication of preference for the female gender and is rejected solely because of his sex, this could constitute discrimination under the LPar. The detail about the male prevalence of the team does not fundamentally change the issue from a legal point of view. It is possible to publish an advertisement addressed to a woman, but once the application of a man has been received, the evaluation must be based on objective criteria of merit, not on gender.
“If sex alone is the reason for exclusion, then it would most likely be discrimination,” Rudolph explained. This principle is central to the protection offered by LPar to Swiss workers.
### The maximum compensation provided by law
Individuals who experience gender discrimination during the hiring process may be able to seek legal compensation. The maximum amount is three monthly salary payments. An important detail: there is no right to get the job. The ruling or recognition of discrimination does not imply an obligation for the company to hire the discriminated candidate, but only to pay financial compensation.

While the issue of gender is relatively clear from a legal point of view, the
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### How to Proceed If Discriminated Against During Hiring
If a candidate believes they have been discriminated against on the basis of gender during the hiring process, they have the opportunity to take action to protect their rights. The first step is to carefully document every communication received from the company and gather evidence demonstrating the reason for the discrimination. Once the evidence has been collected, the candidate may consider filing a complaint with the competent authorities or consulting with a labor law professional to evaluate the available options.
It is important to act promptly, as legal actions are subject to specific deadlines. A legal consultant or attorney specializing in labor law can provide precise guidance on the timeframe for filing an appeal and on the competent jurisdiction.
### Practical Implications for Employers and Candidates
This case involving the Zurich carpentry firm offers an important lesson for all Swiss companies publishing job advertisements. While the law allows for a certain flexibility in the wording of job ads and in the search for specific profiles, employers must be careful not to discriminate against candidates who apply during the evaluation phase.
For candidates, the lesson is equally relevant: if they believe they are discriminated against during the hiring process for reasons protected by federal law (particularly gender), they have legal remedies available. The maximum compensation of three months' salary represents a tangible remedy, even if it does not restore the lost opportunity to obtain the job.
### What Does 'LPar' Protection Really Mean
The Federal Gender Equality Act does not prohibit job advertisements from specifying gender preferences, as confirmed by Rudolph. However, protection kicks in when applications are being evaluated. A company cannot legitimately reject a candidate solely based on gender if they meet the required professional qualifications.
Protection regarding age and other factors remains less defined and more difficult to enforce in a hiring context. This means that many candidates who feel discriminated against for these reasons will find it difficult to obtain effective legal protection unless a systematic pattern of discrimination can be proven.
For those seeking work in Switzerland, the recommendation is to stay informed about your rights. [Read the available job listings](nav:jobs) and, if you feel discriminated against during the selection process on the basis of gender, consider contacting a labor law professional to understand the available options. Federal law is on your side, even if legal proceedings can take time.

On 19 August 2026, the Federal Council communicated the first projection of the federal budget for the current year. The result is surprisingly positive: the Confederation expects a financing surplus of just under 0.8 billion francs, whereas the initial budget projected a deficit of approximately 0.7 billion. This turnaround is mainly driven by growth in revenue from corporate income tax, which had already emerged in early summer based on data from the Cantons and could therefore be taken into account in the 2027 budget.
The improvement was recorded in the ordinary budget, where estimated revenues were revised upwards by 1.9 billion in June. However, the projection also includes an additional credit of 970 million intended for additional military spending — resources needed for air defence systems and protection against mini drones. This increased spending means that ordinary expenditures will also exceed the budgeted amount by 0.8 billion.
### Ordinary and extraordinary budget
In the extraordinary budget, the Confederation benefits from higher revenues from the profit distribution of the Swiss National Bank (SNB), which is 0.3 billion higher than budgeted. In contrast, extraordinary expenditures remain stable at 470 million, corresponding to contributions scheduled for the Cantons to accommodate persons seeking protection from Ukraine. If you wish to understand how your federal tax burden is positioned within the Swiss tax structure, you can use the [federal tax calculator](nav:calculator). According to the Parliament Act (LParl; RS 171.10), the Federal Council is required to carry out two approximate calculations of the expected result of the financial year each year by 30 June and 30 September. The projection is an estimate and should therefore be interpreted with caution, as unforeseen economic situations may alter the final results. ## Corporate Tax Revenues Drive the Budget
The most significant increase concerns corporate income tax, which has risen by 1.4 billion compared to the previous estimate. This growth is concentrated in specific Cantons: Lucerne, Zurich, and Basel-Stadt recorded revenues significantly higher than expected, a phenomenon attributable to a limited number of particularly profitable companies. Geneva, for its part, generated additional temporary revenues from both corporate income tax (+0.2 billion) and income tax (+0.2 billion), added to the 1.2 billion one-off amounts already included in the initial budget, following a review of the cantonal situation in light of the previous year's data.
Beyond corporate income tax, the Confederation also benefits from higher-than-expected revenues from mineral oil tax, with an increase of 0.3 billion. This increase is due to a less pronounced than expected evolution in the spread of electric vehicles, which slows the contraction of revenue from traditional fuels. The overall picture of ordinary revenues thus shows a diversification of positive sources, not limited to corporate profits alone.
### Implications for Taxpayers and Cantons
A positive projection of the federal budget has tangible effects on the Confederation's capacity to finance its competencies and transfer resources to the Cantons. The surplus of 0.8 billion CHF allows greater flexibility in spending decisions, although the additional credit of 970 million for armament absorbs a significant portion of this margin. The decision to invest in air defense and drone protection reflects the Confederation's foreign policy and security priorities in an evolving geopolitical context.

The Federal Council announced on 19 August 2026 a decision destined to revolutionise the wheeled delivery industry in Switzerland. Electric commercial vehicles up to 4.25 tons will receive the same regulatory treatment as traditional vans, breaking down a series of administrative constraints that until now hindered the competitiveness of green mobility in national freight transport.
The decision stems from the examination of the results of the consultation and involves the amendment of as many as five federal ordinances on road traffic. The stated objective is twofold: to pave the way for the spread of electric mobility in the sector and to accelerate the decarbonisation of the delivery sector, a strategic priority for the Confederation in the framework of the transition ### Economic impact on national logistics
Equalization represents a concrete economic catalyst for delivery companies evaluating investments in electric fleets. Until now, a 4-tonne electric van remained subject to heavy vehicle rules: mandatory tachograph, motorway speed restrictions, and driving time constraints. These administrative burdens eroded the margins of ecological and economic advantage compared to traditional combustion models, discouraging the transition even for companies sensitive to sustainability.
With the new legislation entering into force on October 1, 2026, the calculation of operating costs changes radically. A driver of an equalized electric van will be able to:
- Save travel time on long motorway stretches, thanks to the permitted 120 km/h (vs. 100 km/h for traditional heavy vans) - Avoid daily tachograph completion and associated administrative compliance costs - Benefit from less frequent technical maintenance cycles, shortening vehicle downtime - Operate with greater schedule flexibility, thanks to exemptions from work and rest time constraints
These considerations directly affect the profitability of delivery services, especially for couriers and small [logistics companies](nav:companies) operating on repeated national routes (e.g., same-day deliveries from a distribution center to distant cities). Electric mobility thus becomes not only an environmental choice, but an economically rational one for the company budget.

Transitioning to equalized vans will create new [opportunities in the logistics sector](nav:jobs) for drivers specialized in managing electric vehicles. The cantons have a window until February 1, 2028, to align their administrations and control systems with the new federal legislation. This deadline is crucial: it allows the Confederation to coordinate implementation nationwide, while cantonal authorities are expected to update registration procedures, technical inspections, and compliance checks.
Differences between cantons could still persist regarding motor vehicle tax costs or inspection methods, but operational rules will be uniform by February 2028. ## In a nutshell - CET-N proposes to cancel changes to the Lex Koller of the last 40 years - Objective: to curb speculation and reduce land and property prices - The project aims to limit purchases by people residing abroad - Open discussion on stricter restrictions also for EU citizens and border crossers
## Key facts - **What**: Motion to strengthen Lex Koller (LAFE) - When: Proposal discussed by the CET-N, with review by the Federal Council - Where: Switzerland - Who: National Economic and Tax Commission (CET-N) - Amount: Over 1.5 million net immigration since 2002
The National Economic and Tax Commission (CET-N) has adopted a motion that marks a potential return to the past for the Swiss property market. The parliamentary act, promoted by National Councillor Thomas Aeschi (UDC/ZG), asks to annul all the changes made to the "Lex Koller" in the last fortyyears. The declared intention is to restore the regulatory situation prior to 1985, by acting on the federal law on the purchase of funds by people abroad (LAFE). The main reason given by the parliamentarian concerns the growing difficulties that middle-class families encounter in trying to buy a home. This criticality also involves small and medium-sized enterprises, often looking for suitable spaces for their operational activities.
According to the analysis proposed by Aeschi, The revision project of the 'Lex Koller' presented by the Federal Council outlines a significant change in the authorization regime for real estate purchases. The new provisions aim to specifically target foreign demand by introducing stricter constraints for commercial and residential properties. Regarding commercial real estate, residents abroad would no longer have the right to purchase them for rental purposes, being able to maintain the purchase without authorization only if intended for direct use in their own business. This measure directly affects the management of real estate assets by international entities.
### Impact on real estate and financial companies A further pillar of the crackdown concerns the general prohibition for foreigners to purchase listed shares of residential real estate companies. The restriction extends to regularly traded shares of real estate funds and SICAVs, financial instruments that have so far allowed foreign investors to access the Swiss market by bypassing the classic limitations of the law. Analyzing the positions that emerged during the consultation that ended in July, a clear divide is evident. While on one hand the SP and the SVP welcome the tightening, seeing it as a necessary bulwark to protect the purchasing power of tenants and those looking for homes, on the other hand, The Centre and real estate companies warn about the possible negative repercussions on the national economic system. The fear is that overly rigid regulation could slow down investments in an already complex sector.
The Swiss Group for Mountain Regions (SAB) has raised specific objections, arguing that such plans could damage the economy of alpine regions without providing a concrete solution to the housing shortage. According to the SAB and The Centre, the roots of the housing problem should not be sought exclusively in foreign demand, but rather in procedural delays and restrictive building regulations that hinder territorial planning. The divergence of views highlights how the issue of access to housing is closely linked to land management and urban densification policies. In this scenario of regulatory uncertainty, those planning investments or real estate purchases must carefully monitor parliamentary developments, as final decisions could significantly alter the requirements needed to operate in the Swiss real estate market, influencing both private individuals and industry professionals who need [information on the cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) to evaluate their investments.

item.description: 20-minute survey/Tamedia: 62% of Swiss against the neutrality initiative. But Ticino votes yes with 52%. Vote on 27 September 2026.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - 20-minute survey/Tamedia of 12-13 August 2026: 62% of Swiss against the neutrality initiative - Ticino is the exception with 52% in favour, the only canton where initiative would pass - Feeding initiative rejected: 65% against, 31% in favour - Vote on September 27, 2026
## Key facts - **What**: Survey on two federal initiatives (neutrality and nutrition) - When: 12-13 August 2026 (detection), processing 13-17 August, vote 27 September 2026 - Where: German Switzerland, French Switzerland, Ticino - Who: 20 minutes/Tamedia, 13,154 participants - Neutrality results: 36% yes / 62% no; Power supply: 31% yes / 65% no
The first 20-minute survey/Tamedia on the two initiatives on the ballot on 27 September 2026 reveals a clear opposition of the Swiss population to both proposals. For the neutrality initiative, 62% are against the requested change, while only 36% support it. The remaining 2% remains undecided. The initiative on food has even less consensus: 31% in favour against 65% against, with 4% undecided.
But the most surprising fact concerns the regional differences. While German Switzerland and Romanian Switzerland clearly reject both initiatives, Ticino stands out from the rest of the country on the issue of neutrality: in our canton, the initiative would pass with 52% approval, against 45% against. It is a result at odds with the ### Ticino against the rest of Switzerland
The Ticino result on the neutrality initiative represents a resounding exception in the Swiss landscape. This gap highlights a Röstigraben that is not only linguistic but also political on a central issue for Switzerland. Proponents of the neutrality initiative argue that enshrining neutrality in the Constitution would prevent the Federal Council and politicians from weakening or interpreting it at their own discretion. They see a stricter constitutional wording as a guarantee against gradual changes in Swiss foreign policy.
Those who oppose the initiative, on the other hand, put forward arguments based on the Swiss tradition of openness and dialogue. According to the opponents, the initiative would severely limit Switzerland's ability to act in the face of global foreign policy challenges. Renouncing sanctions in the event of violations of international law could be seen as taking a stand in favor of aggressor states and damage Switzerland's reputation in the world. Finally, a rigid conception of neutrality would entail the sacrifice of cooperation in matters of security and defense, weakening the country's defensive capacity.
### Food supply: less divided, but still rejected
The food supply initiative shows a radically different situation. 65% of respondents oppose it, while 31% support the proposal and 4% remain undecided. Unlike the neutrality issue, no significant Röstigraben emerges: the entire national electorate moves with relative uniformity in its rejection. German-speaking Switzerland expresses 70% 'no' (27% 'yes'), French-speaking Switzerland 58% 'no' (37% 'yes'), and Ticino 50% 'no' (45% 'yes').
The only electorate that shows broad support is that of the Greens, with 69% in favor. The base of the PS appears divided instead: 46% support the initiative while 50% reject it. In all other parties, the opposition is marked: GLP (66%), SVP (74%), The Centre (75%), and FDP (83%). Gender and age also have an impact: the 'no' is more widespread among men (70%) than among women (59%), and retirees reach 74% in opposition.
### What proponents and opponents are asking for
Those who support the food supply initiative do not express a single dominant argument. 31% cite the possibility of achieving a higher degree of food self-sufficiency, thus reducing dependence on foreign countries in the event of a crisis — a legitimate concern considering how decisions on food affect the [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living). 28% point instead to the protection of groundwater resources from pollution caused by fertilizers and pesticides. The main reason for opposition to the initiative, cited by 46% of opponents, concerns the 70% self-sufficiency target contained in the proposal. According to this criticism, the measure would end up turning into a 'state-imposed menu', leaving very little room for animal-based products and severely limiting consumer choices.

item.title: Asylum seekers resume transfers to Italy
item.description: Switzerland will resume transfers of asylum seekers to Italy, after almost four years of blockade.
item.content:encoded:
Switzerland will resume transfers of asylum seekers to Italy, after almost four years of blockade. Transfers will be managed gradually, as confirmed by the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM). The resumption of transfers is linked to the new European Pact on Migration and Asylum, which entered into force on 12 June.
The decision was taken after a long period of negotiations between Switzerland and the European Union. SEM confirmed that the transfers will resume shortly, but did not provide an exact date. 📊
The new European Pact on Migration and Asylum provides for the resumption of transfers of asylum seekers between EU Member States. Switzerland, not being a member of the EU, had to negotiate a specific agreement to join this pact. The agreement was signed on 26 June and enters into force on 12 June.
The resumption of transfers is an important new development for Switzerland, which has had to deal with the crisis of asylum seekers in recent years. According to SEM data, in 2020 about 43,000 asylum seekers were registered in Switzerland, while in 2021 the number fell to about 26,000. The decrease was attributed to the crisis of asylum seekers and their greater mobility to other countries.
The resumption of transfers will be managed gradually, to avoid creating reception and integration problems for asylum seekers. SEM announced that the The resumption of transfers of asylum seekers to Italy is linked to the new European Pact on Migration and Asylum, which provides financial support and other discounts for countries of arrival, such as Italy. Switzerland could now return only 652 people to Italy, as almost 40% of asylum seekers have obtained protection in Switzerland.
According to data from the Federal Office of Legal Affairs (UJU), between 2020 and 2022, 1,454 asylum seekers were repatriated to Italy, worth 24.5 million francs. However, due to the failure to ratify the European Pact on Migration and Asylum, Switzerland was forced to suspend the transfers.
With the ratification of the European Pact on Migration and Asylum, Switzerland could now return up to 652 people a year to Italy. This means that Switzerland could return to Italy about 30% of asylum seekers who have obtained protection in Switzerland. 📊
The European Pact on Migration and Asylum also provides financial support for countries of arrival, such as Italy. Switzerland could contribute 20 million francs per year to support the countries of arrival.
